newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spanish inflation drops to 29-year low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spanish inflation drops to 29-year low.

text.p: Spanish inflation fell to its lowest level in 29 years in March, raising analysts' expectations for further interest rate cuts and bolstering Spain's ambitions to make the first wave of a single European currency.

The National Statistics Institute (INE) reported on Friday that the consumer price index (CPI) rose a modest 0.1 percent in March, to give a 2.2 percent rise on the year. This compares with a 2.5 percent year-on-year rate in February and 2.9 percent in January.

"This is very good data which shows that prices in the real economy are decelerating .... it opens the way for the Bank of Spain to cut 25 basis points this month," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

The data was at the low end of expectations. A Reuters poll of analysts had predicted inflation to rise 0.24 percent on the month and 2.4 percent on the year, and the news prompted some to downgrade their 1997 estimates.

"March CPI data was another positive surprise...at the end of the year we see inflation around two percent or below, completing the Bank of Spain's inflation objective for 1997 and 1998," Banco Central Hispano said in a statement.

Analysts said the data could prompt the Bank of Spain to sanction its third official money market rate cut of the year as soon as April 15 at its regular repurchase auction. The central bank last cut its official rate on March 14 to 5.75 percent.

"It's clear (the Bank of Spain) has room to cut rates by 25 basis points in the next month and whether or not it cuts next week will depend on market expectations and the position of the peseta," said Antonio Villarroya, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
Others forecast bolder action over the coming months.

"Given the likely performance of the inflation rate over the next couple of months, there's no reason why we can't see the repo rate down to five percent," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase Investment Bank in London, speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

The data also bolsters the likelihood that Spain will meet inflation requirements for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and increases the probability it will undershoot the government's goal to end the year at a rate of 2.6 percent.
"This data helps build the credibility of Spain to make EMU," said Urrutia.

The government said the inflation rate had now stabilised to within the limits laid out in the Maastricht Treaty, which stipulates that it be no more than 1.5 percent above the average of the three best performances in the EU.
"The positive evolution of the inflation rate means that we have reached our objectives for the year in the first three months," the Economy Ministry said in a statement.
March core inflation, which excludes volatile fresh food and energy prices, also hit new lows with a 2.1 percent rise on the year, the lowest level since INE began recording this component in 1992.
The food sector was key to subduing March inflation, analysts said.

"Foods have performed positively despite the rise in the price of tobacco in March. We're in a good position to see new falls in the next few months and in principle that leads us to think that CPI may break the two percent barrier in May," said Antonio Miguelanez, economist at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya in Madrid.
"There's still resistance in the goods and services prices to go down. We'll have to wait and see the effects of the liberalisation measures approved by the government," said Merrill's Villarroya.
